The Arabic script is used to write the Arabic language and several other languages across the Middle East and North Africa. It consists of 28 letters, most of which are consonants. Arabic is written from right to left.

The Arabic alphabet includes letters that change shape based on their position in a word (initial, medial, final, or standalone). There are also different forms of some letters used at the beginning or middle of a word versus when they appear at the end.

The script is cursive, meaning that most letters connect to the letters before and after them within a word. Vowels are generally not written as individual letters but are represented using diacritical marks (like short lines and dots) above or below consonants.

Arabic script is used for various languages, and additional letters or modifications may be added to accommodate specific sounds in different languages.

Learning Arabic script involves understanding the shapes and positions of the letters, their different forms, and how they connect to form words. It's a beautifully intricate writing system with its own unique calligraphic styles.
